---
title: "Functions and approximations"
subtitle: "Otto & Day, primer 1, with PracticalCAS"
engine: julia
---

The first primer collects the calculus used throughout the book: derivatives,
limits, Taylor approximations, logarithms and exponentials, and sums. Each has
a direct counterpart here.

```{julia}
using PracticalCAS
@syms x t r::positive K::positive a::positive b::positive n::positive
```

## Derivatives and maxima

The per-capita birth rate `b(n) = a n exp(-b n)` peaks where its derivative
vanishes; the second derivative confirms a maximum.

```{julia}
f = a * n * exp(-b * n)
crit = solve(diff(f, n), n)
```

```{julia}
simplify(subs(diff(f, n, 2), n => crit[1]))
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(only(crit), 1 / b)
@assert isnegative(simplify(subs(diff(f, n, 2), n => 1 / b)))
```

## Limits

Limits describe long-term behaviour and the values of expressions where they
are formally undefined (by L'Hôpital's rule):

```{julia}
limit(K * n / (K + n), n, ∞), limit((exp(r * t) - 1) / t, t, 0)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert limit(K * n / (K + n), n, ∞) == K
@assert isequiv(limit((exp(r * t) - 1) / t, t, 0), r)
```

## Taylor approximations

Near `x = 0`, `log(1 + x) ≈ x - x²/2` and `exp(x) ≈ 1 + x`. The approximation
`(1 + r)ᵗ ≈ exp(r t)` for small `r` is why discrete and continuous growth
models agree when changes per step are small.

```{julia}
taylor(log(1 + x), x, 0, 3), taylor(exp(x), x, 0, 2)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(taylor(log(1 + x), x, 0, 3), x - x^2 / 2 + x^3 / 3)
```

A function of two variables has a multivariate Taylor expansion; to first
order it is the linear approximation used in every stability analysis.

```{julia}
@syms y
linearize(x * exp(y), [x, y], [1, 0])
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(linearize(x * exp(y), [x, y], [1, 0]), x + y)
```

## Exponentials and logarithms

Doubling time of exponential growth: solve `exp(r t) = 2`.

```{julia}
solve(exp(r * t) ~ 2, t)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(only(solve(exp(r * t) ~ 2, t)), log(toterm(2)) / r)

```

## Sums

Geometric series appear in models with immigration and in probability. Sums
of powers have closed forms too.

```{julia}
@syms k::natural T::natural q
summation(q^k, k, 0, T - 1), summation(k, k, 1, T)
```

```{julia}
summation(q^k, k, 0, ∞)          # valid for |q| < 1
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(summation(q^k, k, 0, T - 1), (q^T - 1) / (q - 1))
@assert isequiv(summation(k, k, 1, T), T * (T + 1) / 2)
@assert isequiv(summation(q^k, k, 0, ∞), 1 / (1 - q))
```

Factorials and binomial coefficients are symbolic functions;
`binomial(n, 2)` is the number of pairs.

```{julia}
@syms m::natural
binomial(m, 2), simplify(factorial(m + 2) / factorial(m))
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(binomial(m, 2), m * (m - 1) / 2)
@assert isequiv(simplify(factorial(m + 2) / factorial(m)), (m + 1) * (m + 2))
```

## Integrals

Integrals give the total from a rate, and normalising constants:

```{julia}
integrate(r * exp(-r * t), t, 0, ∞), integrate(exp(-x^2 / 2), x, -∞, ∞)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert integrate(r * exp(-r * t), t, 0, ∞) == 1
@assert isequiv(integrate(exp(-x^2 / 2), x, -∞, ∞), sqrt(2 * PracticalCAS.PI))
```
